beats.text: You are driving, and your navigation app suggests a route.
But there is an emergency ahead, and the road is closed. The app cannot see it. You can.
So you do not follow it blindly. You take another road. That is what a clinician must be able to do with AI: understand it, question it, and override it.
This is augmented intelligence. Automation hands the work to the machine. Augmentation helps the human do the work better.
The AI brings speed, pattern detection and consistent calculation. The clinician brings the examination, communication, values, and ethical judgment.
So how much should you trust the AI? Picture a dial.
Turn it all the way up, and you get automation bias: accepting the suggestion just because it looks confident, even when your own evidence disagrees.
That leads to commission errors: doing something wrong, because the system suggested it.
And omission errors: failing to act, because the system did not warn you.
Turn it all the way down, and you get under-trust: ignoring support that was correct and useful.
The goal is in the middle. Calibrated trust: trust that matches what the system can really do, with healthy scepticism.
And for that, oversight has to be meaningful. The clinician needs time, the right information, and the authority to disagree. Not a rubber stamp.
